newsitem.title: USA: BASEBALL-AUSTRALIAN LLOYD LIVES AMERICAN DREAM WITH SERIES TITLE.
newsitem.headline: BASEBALL-AUSTRALIAN LLOYD LIVES AMERICAN DREAM WITH SERIES TITLE.

text.p: Graeme Lloyd, dripping with champagne from a wild locker room celebration, said it was the thrill of a lifetime to be the first Australian to be fitted for a World Series ring following the Yankee triumph Saturday.
"It's amazing, outstanding," said the left-handed reliever, who helped pitch New York out of a sixth-inning jam in their 3-2 clinching win over the Atlanta Braves in Game 6.
"It's magical. The feelings I've had will never be repeated. The feeling of running around the field, the feeling of satisfaction to have my mom and dad here."
The celebration started with a huge pile-up at the pitcher's mound with riot police lining up in a "V" formation to protect them.

But with Darryl Strawberry leading the way, the Yankees broke through the police and ran a victory lap around the stadium to delirious cheers from a crowd of 56,375 celebrating the Yanks' first Series title in 18 years.
On their way off the field, the Yankees hurled fielding mitts, batting gloves and caps into the stands to reward the fans.
In the clubhouse, Lloyd was asked if there was an Australian equivalent.
"The Melbourne Cup, no, no -- Australian Rules Football Grand Final," he said. "They have 100,000 in that stadium. But everybody is moving around, so they can't pick out anybody and boo them."

Lloyd heard plenty of boos after he first joined the Yankees in a trade with the Milwaukee Brewers. A sore elbow rendered him ineffective, and the Yankees filed a protest claiming they had received damaged goods.
But after a cortisone shot and some rest, Lloyd recovered his form and turned out to be a key ingredient in the dominant relief corps that set the Yankees apart from their post-season opponents.

In the Series-clincher, Lloyd retired pinch-hitter Ryan Klesko on a pop-up to second with runners on first and third and two out in the sixth to preserve the Yankees' lead. In four Series appearances he went 2 2/3 innings without yielding a hit or a run, and struck out four without issuing a walk.

Making his triumph even more special was the presence of his parents, Noel and Pauline, who made the trip from their sheep farm in Geelong, some 50 miles from Melbourne, to watch Lloyd pitch in the post-season.
Pauline Lloyd gave her son high marks for poise. "He's been surprisingly calm and focused," she said.
"He's gone through a hectic time but come through with flying colours," said a beaming Noel Lloyd, who has followed the Yankees all through their October run to the Series crown.
"To see his club win is just fantastic."
